#2592. Sebastian Grønning explains how Hertha have turned things around in Berlin

After several turbulent years, Hertha finally appear to be moving in the right direction. Following relegation from the Bundesliga in 2023 and successive campaigns in which promotion proved elusive, the capital club have made an excellent start to the new 2. Bundesliga season.

Hertha sit top of the table after 11 matches, having won 10 of their opening 11 fixtures, and the feeling around the Olympiastadion is increasingly one of optimism.

Speaking in an interview with Bundesliga media, Grønning admitted that such a flying start was not necessarily expected following a summer of significant squad changes. However, the early performances quickly gave the players belief that something special was developing.

“From the friendly matches and then from the first two competitive games of the season, we got the feeling that, hey, we really have something here that we can build on,” Grønning explained.

“That confidence boost from game to game and from win to win has naturally given us that boost and that confidence in believing that we’re doing something right here.”

For the striker, one of the biggest differences compared to previous campaigns has been the clarity within the squad, with every player understanding their individual responsibilities.

“I would say our philosophy is quite clear for every player in the team. We know what role each one of us has, what we have to bring and what we have to do,” he continued.

“When we put all these roles together, I think we have a very good harmony and very good chemistry in the team.”

Grønning also highlighted Hertha’s physical intensity, believing their ability to maintain an attacking approach even when protecting leads has helped distinguish them from their promotion rivals.

A significant part of Hertha’s transformation has been the influence of head coach Stefan Leitl, who has now had the opportunity to shape the squad more closely around his footballing philosophy.

Grønning was particularly complimentary of the 49-year-old, praising his tactical understanding, communication and ability to recognise the strengths of his players.

“He’s really good at recognising what kinds of players he has and to build the team around these players. Then he’s a very clear communicator,” the striker said.

After arriving in Berlin towards the end of the 2024/25 season and having overseen several key departures amid financial uncertainty, Leitl has now used this summer to put his stamp on the squad. Grønning believes the current group is much more representative of the coach’s ideas following significant recruitment activity.

“I think this year he had a bigger impact in terms of recruiting players, in terms of the style and to fit these together. So I think it’s fair to say that this is more his team.”

The Danish forward also made it clear that he has personally embraced Leitl’s approach, suggesting the coach has earned the trust of the dressing room.

“I’m really buying into how we want to do things this year. And I’m really buying into his ideas. I want to play for him really very much.”

Despite the remarkable start, Grønning recognises that the relationship between Hertha and their supporters has been shaped by several years of disappointment.

The club’s relegation in 2023 has been followed by three frustrating seasons in the 2. Bundesliga, with hopes of a return to the top flight failing to materialise each time.

Consequently, while improved performances have brought renewed excitement to the Olympiastadion, the striker believes everyone must remain patient rather than getting carried away with promotion expectations.

“I also think the fans heard it from the past and have these scars of believing in the best outcome, and Hertha can get them hurt or disappointed, you know?” he admitted.

Grønning believes the only way to change that narrative is through continued performances on the pitch.

“Both the fans and us as a team have to just stay calm and keep following this path of focusing on each game and putting that energy and effort into it.”

Nevertheless, the opportunity to be part of a Hertha side that finally secures promotion is clearly something that motivates him.

“Every player feels the same as me that it would be great if I could be a part of that team that brings Hertha back where they belong,” Grønning explained.

“They deserve to be in the Bundesliga and fans deserve to see Bundesliga football.”

However, he was quick to acknowledge that there is still a long way to go, with plenty of challenges remaining before promotion becomes a reality.

On a personal level, the Danish striker is also determined to keep developing his game, having established himself as a traditional centre-forward whose greatest strengths lie in his positioning, movement and finishing inside the penalty area.

“I’m a classic box striker. I need to have service in the box. I’m very strong in and around the box with my finishing, with my positioning, with my timing,” he explained.

Grønning also revealed that he regularly stays behind after training to work on his finishing, highlighting the attention to detail within Hertha’s coaching setup.

Even after finding the net, however, he insists there is no room for complacency.

“It’s not that after a goal everything is good and everything is positive. So it’s just about the process and you have to trust that,” he added.

For Hertha, that mentality perhaps reflects the wider approach currently being adopted in Berlin. There is renewed confidence, a clear identity and a squad that appears increasingly comfortable with its responsibilities.

The memories of previous disappointments have not disappeared, but with Hertha leading the 2. Bundesliga after 11 matches, the foundations for a genuine promotion challenge are beginning to look increasingly convincing.

#2589. Rams star Aaron Donald records first sack since coming out of retirement in game vs. Cardinals

Aaron Donald, for the first time in nearly three years, has sacked a quarterback.

The Los Angeles Rams star, who came out of retirement earlier this fall to rejoin the franchise, brought down Arizona Cardinals quarterback Carson Beck early in the second quarter of their matchup on Sunday afternoon. It marked his first sack since Dec. 31, 2023, or 1,050 days ago.

The sack forced a fourth down, and got the Rams the ball back in the contest at State Farm Stadium.

Donald retired shortly after his final sack in 2023. He finished with 53 total tackles and eight sacks in that campaign. Earlier this fall, after rumors for weeks, Donald rejoined the Rams to team up with fellow defensive star Myles Garrett and bolster the Rams' chances at making a deep postseason run.

The 35-year-old made his debut on Sept. 21 in a win over the New York Giants, and had three tackles in that contest. While he's been impressive in his return, especially considering he had been away from the game for so long, Donald failed to record a sack in his first seven games this fall. Donald entered Sunday's contest with 13 total tackles, including seven solo.

The sack on Sunday marked the 112th of his career. That's good for 42nd on the league's all-time list. While he's well back from the 200 that leader Bruce Smith recorded in his career, there are only seven active players in the NFL with more sacks than Donald has.

The Rams, who will have a bye next week, carried a 5-4 record into Sunday's game in Arizona. They've won three straight, however, and finally got above .500 for the first time all season with their 20-13 win over the Washington Commanders last week.

Though the Rams still have a long way to go to actually make a run at another ring, Donald finally getting his first sack out of the way is a big step for him in his comeback.

#2586. Embiid-less Sixers get just enough from center position in win vs. Pacers

It's been awhile since we saw a 1 p.m. win on a Sunday in this city. The Sixers knocked off the Indiana Pacers 131-124 Sunday Afternoon.

Jaylen Brown powered the Sixers with 31 points shooting 12-of-18 from the floor along with three rebounds. Tyrese Maxey quietly put up 27 points and six assists shooting 9-of-19 from the field.

LeBron James had a tremendous day sharing the rock as his 11 assists moved him up to third in the league's all-time assist leaders. He also had 15 points and six rebounds on 5-of-8 shooting. VJ Edgecombe bounced back from a scoreless first half to end with 11 points, four rebounds, and six assists shooting 5-of-11 from the floor. Pascal Siakam led the Pacers with 31 as well.

Joel Embiid was out with plantar fascia management in his right foot, along with Adem Bona and Dominick Barlow. The Pacers were missing Tyrese Haliburton, Andrew Nembhard and Ben Sheppard.

The Sixers moved the ball very well on their opening possession of the game as Maxey got wide open on a cut, but he smoked the bunny. It looked like he might not have corralled the bounce pass from LeBron. Maxey did get the Sixers on the board running quick off the ensuing Pacers miss. Brown knocked down two of his first three jumpers as the two of them accounted for Philly's first 15 points of the game.

A lot of what Maxey was able to get early was set up by LeBron, who was zipping the ball all around the perimeter early. Maxey took full advantage and had a lot of space to get his first two three-pointers off. Maxey found James up ahead for a transition bucket for James' first points of the day.

Brown had a really good jump shooting quarter, putting up 11 in the first. He didn't seem to have a hard time getting to his pull-up spots, and knocked them down whether there was a hand in his face or not. Meanwhile on the other end, all five of the Pacers' starters scored within the first six minutes of the game and started the game 11-of-19 from the floor. They were already taking advantage of the small Sixers team available with nine early second-chance points on four offensive rebounds.

Kelly Oubre Jr. was playing in Philly for the first time since signing with the Pacers, and got off to a good start. He scored seven in the first, beating his old team on a couple of cuts. Another old friend, T.J. McConnell, hit a few of his classic short pull-up jumpers. The Sixers trailed by six after the Pacers shot 62% from the field in the first.

A quick rest on the bench didn't cool Brown down as he nailed two more jumpers to star the second. After getting some minutes in Delaware over the weekend, Labaron Philon Jr. was back in the rotation, checking in early in the second, even if it was because Anfernee Simons picked up two quick fouls. The first time he got into an action was LeBron screening and rolling for him, but the play was quickly whistled dead when Quentin Jackson got into it with James. A couple possessions later James hit Philon on the wing for a three.

Regardless of whether the Sixers had Jabari Walker on the floor or a less traditional center option, they had trouble giving the Pacers any resistance at the rim. Fourteen of Indy's first 16 points in the second came from the paint or getting fouled in the paint. With that shot diet it wasn't a shock they continued to hover over 60% from the field.

Brown continued to find ways to put the ball in the basket, and the Sixers needed every bit of it to keep pace. There was even a sequence where he grabbed a rebound from the floor despite getting hit in the face earlier in the possession.

After a couple of fast breaks Maxey simply created with his speed. James threw a brilliant bounce pass down the baseline to Brown for another fast break that capped off a 16-4 Sixer run. Coming out of a Pacer timeout, Oubre drew a foul on a Brown push-off, something Oubre really exaggerated in celebration. Aaron Nesmith scored a basket out of that, but Oubre missed the corner three the Pacers got out of a Maxey turnover their next trip down the floor.

LeBron took that rebound and got up the floor quickly for a dunk attempt before the half but Oubre fouled him hard to avoid that. James hit the deck hard and stayed down for a bit, but eventually got up and knocked down two free throws to put the Sixers up by one at the break. Whether it was related or not, James and Maxey had a lengthy discussion with Tyrese Haliburton before heading back to the locker room.

Going scoreless in the first half, Edgecombe just could not buy a bucket. He missed another open corner three early in the third, but did start to produce. He nabbed a steal to start the quarter and found Maxey for a three, then finally got a couple of baskets himself going to the basket. He tried his damndest to put Ivica Zubac on a poster, but Zubac got over with enough time to meet Edgecombe with a hard foul.

A center with a clear height advantage like Zubac was always going to give Walker trouble defensively, but he was putting in another good shift of hardwork. On top of pulling down four defensive rebounds and two on the offensive end, Walker had drilled three threes which is always a nice help to the offense.

With that being said, Nick Nurse decided to give Tacko Fall his frst real minutes when Walker went to the bench. Fall rebounded Edgecombe's missed free throw, which once again sent the crowd into a wild frenzy. They also ate up every bit of the screen he set for LeBron as James scored eight straight for the Sixers.

There were some rusty moments like a foul and a defensive three-second violation, but the Fall minutes definitely could have gone worse defensively. Multiple shots at the rim were altered by him being there, including a layup attempt that went out of bounds over the backboard.

Their defense to close the quarter looked more comfortable. Dean Wade made a great play to stop a fastbreak, and Kentavious Caldwell-Pope fought for a loose ball that led to him earning a pair of free throws. Maxey fell into a rhythm again on the other end, hitting a floater and another stepback three. Simons hit his second quarter-ending buzzer-beater in as many games, giving the Sixers a 10-point lead after the third.

After such a strong first half Brown had to sit most of the third quarter when he quickly picked up his third foul. That long rest didn't slow his momentum down though as he hit a pull-up to start the quarter before trailing LeBron to hit an open three off the catch.

A few possessions later Edgecombe made a nice read to open up Wade in the corner, setting the Sixers up to good position to start running away with the game. A three from Josh Huff followed by two consecutive and-1s by Siakam made sure that this game was far from over. The Sixers responded with a possession of great ball movement that, as the tweet below points out, was entirely orchestrated by LeBron, and led to another Wade three. However Siakam answered again by getting right to the basket and would pick up another and-1 two possessions later.

The Sixers' offense did stagnate a bit, especially when LeBron went to the bench. They were lucky they weren't punished more during their two minutes scoreless stretch. The only time they stopped Siakam in this stretch was when he pulled up for a jumper. Brown was finally able to snap that with a midrange but the Pacers were still able to chop the lead to four. KCP hit a big three to push that lead back up as LeBron was waiting to check back in.

James threw another dime to a baseline cutter on his first possession back in the game, and Wade was able to draw a foul as he finished the dunk, putting the Sixers back up by double-digits with just over two to go. After Brown split a pair of free throws, Siakam got another and-1. He missed the free throw, and after each team committed an offensive foul, that pretty much put the Pacers in fouling territory from there on out.

#2583. Nikita Kucherov trade request: Five potential landing spots for the reigning NHL MVP

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

One of the greatest players in Tampa Bay Lightning history may soon be wearing a different jersey. According to Sportsnet, Nikita Kucherov has told the Lightning he won't sign a contract extension and has requested a trade.

Kucherov, a two-time Stanley Cup champion and two-time Hart Trophy winner as league MVP, is one of the best players of his era. The 33-year-old just passed the legendary Steven Stamkos for the all-time franchise lead in points and has shown no signs of slowing down.

Just last season, Kucherov posted 44 goals and 86 assists en route to his second Hart Trophy win. His underlying numbers were even better with a five-on-five goal differential of plus-38 and an expected goals share of 57.0 percent. Only a select few players can drive play from the wing like Kucherov, and that makes him a unicorn of sorts.

Kucherov is in the final year of a contract that pays him $9.5 million per season, and with the salary cap rising rapidly, he's due for a gargantuan raise next summer. It sounds like Kucherov and the Lightning were too far apart on that number, so the superstar winger has shifted his focuse to a change of scenery.

It's important to note that Kucherov has limited trade protection in the form of a 10-team trade list, but that should be more than enough for the Lightning to find a suitable trade partner. With that in mind, let's take a look at five teams that would be ideal fits for Kucherov as he prepares for the next chapter of his illustrious career.

Right out of the gate, this is the most natural fit of all the potential landing spots. General manager Kent Hughes has done a superb job of locking down his young core on team-friendly contracts, and as a result, the Canadiens have nearly $30 million in projected cap space for next season. They also have a glaring need in their top two lines, and I'd say the reigning Hart Trophy winner would fill that role quite nicely.

Montreal's moment to strike is now. It's an ascendant team with a great salary cap situtation and assets to spend. It's time to make a splash, and this would be a tsunami. Just imagine Kucherov on a power play unit with Nick Suzuki, Cole Caufield, Lane Hutson and Ivan Demidov. Kucherov would also be coached by former Lightning teammate Martin St. Louis, so a rapport would already exist between player and coach. I expect the Canadiens to do everything in their power to land Kucherov.

We already know the Wild are big-game hunting at forward because they've been heavily linked to former Detroit Red Wings captain Dylan Larkin. If I were advising general manager Bill Guerin -- and I'm certainly not -- I would recommend Minnesota package whatever assets it has offered Detroit and redirect them to Tampa Bay. No, Kucherov is not a center,  and that's the Wild's biggest need.

However, Kucherov is a rare breed of winger in that he can drive play better than most first-line centers from the wing. Put him on a line with Kirill Kaprizov, and the only time opponents will touch the puck is when they're pulling out of the net.

With Quinn Hughes also on an expiring contract, acquiring Kucherov would be a risky move for the Wild. What if they give up premium assets only to lose Kucherov and Hughes next summer? I don't think fear can dictate Minnesota's decisions. The team has a top-two defenseman in the world on its roster right now, and it has the opportunity to acquire a top-five forward. Worry about next summer when the time comes. Go all in to win the Cup while you have a chance.

It was no secret that the Hurricanes were in on the Connor Hellebuyck sweepstakes but just missed out. So, if they can't get better at preventing goals, why not get much better at scoring them? Carolina doesn't exactly need any help offensively, but adding Kucherov would go a long way to helping the team repeat as Stanley Cup champions. Besides, Kucherov would provide another level of playmaking and finishing that the Canes don't currently have on their roster.

Carolina has a good chunk of cap space available already, and it wouldn't need to shed much in order to make room for Kucherov. The Canes also have some enticing young players on their roster that might appeal to the Bolts, and they have three first-round picks over the next two drafts. Why not take a shot at landing a superstar winger?

Similar to the Hurricanes, the Mammoth were in the mix to acquire Hellebucyk, and for good reason. The goaltending tandem of Karel Vejmelka and Sebastian Cossa has not been good, so Utah may have to outscore its problems until one of the goalies finds a groove. Offense may be the best defense for the Mammoth -- and if that's the case -- then Kucherov should be in the mix for the Norris Trophy. There is a great young core of forwards in Salt Lake City, and I think Kucherov would be a perfect fit alongside Logan Cooley, who is emerging as a franchise center.

Utah also has plenty of draft capital with which to work, and it's projected for just over $25 million in salary cap space next season. The Mammoth don't have any major pending free agents on their cap sheet, so they're a suitor capable of signing Kucherov to a long-term extension.

Allow me to get a little bold on the fifth and final destination. The Stars have already failed to sign 27-year-old winger Jason Robertson to a long-term extension once. The two sides agreed to a one-year deal worth $12 million prior to the season, but Robertson's future with the team is still very much in doubt. What if Dallas and Tampa Bay executed a true "hockey trade" -- one player for one player?

Dallas would get the better player in Kucherov, but there are no guarantees regarding an extension. The Stars are in win-now mode, and Kucherov could help them get over the Cup hump immediately. Tampa Bay would get a younger player in Robertson, and although he doesn't have the elite playmaking ability of Kucherov, he's still an exceptionally talented scorer. Perhaps the Bolts could get him to join the team's core and sign a multi-year contract. This deal could work for both sides.

#2582. LeBron James moves past Jason Kidd for 3rd on NBA’s career assist list, 76ers top Pacers 131-124

PHILADELPHIA — LeBron James had 11 assists and moved into third on the NBA's career list, and he added 15 points and six rebounds to lead the Philadelphia 76ers past the Indiana Pacers 131-124 on Sunday.

James, who turns 42 next month, dished one to VJ Edgecombe in the fourth quarter for assist 12,092 to pass Jason Kidd on the career list. John Stockton and Chris Paul are 1-2 in NBA history.

Jaylen Brown scored 31 points and Tyrese Maxey added 27 for the Sixers.

Pascal Siakam led the Pacers with 31 points and former Sixer Kelly Oubre Jr. added 16.

James continued an early habit in his first season with the Sixers by picking his spot to take control of a game.

This one came in the third quarter, right after Sixers fans went wild when seldom-used 7-foot-6 center Tacko Fall checked into the game. James immediately went to work picking apart the Pacers and scored eight straight points to give them an 82-73 lead.

Signed ahead of training camp for backcourt depth, Fall almost immediately strained his left hip and missed the preseason. Coach Nick Nurse said ahead of Sunday's game he still thought the fan-favorite Fall could help the Sixers, but that he had "seen him out there, some form," and that "I might just have to take that leap."

Fall helped in that pivotal third-quarter stretch for James. Fall grabbed an offensive rebound that led to a possession where James would sink two from the free-throw line. James then added a near-uncontested driving layup because of a perfect screen from Fall. James added a 20-footer and a dunk during the run.

Fall grabbed two offensive rebounds in 3 minutes. His final stat line with no points in 5 minutes might be easy to overlook — unlike the towering Fall — but he had a major impact in pushing the Sixers to 11-3.

Joel Embiid sat out for the Sixers in the first set of back-to-back games. A two-time NBA scoring champion, Embiid should return to the lineup Monday at Brooklyn. James is another veteran who generally does not play in back-to-back games and seemed poised to take his turn sitting out against the Nets.

James took a hard foul when he drove the lane against Oubre in the first quarter. James clutched his left wrist for a moment but appeared to show no ill effects the rest of the game.

#2581. No. 1 South Carolina vs. No. 3 USC takeaways: Gamecocks once again show their mettle

The No. 1 Gamecocks held off the resurgent No. 3 Southern Cal Trojans, 89-85, in the second installment of "The Real SC" series between schools with the same acronym on opposite coasts. The game was played at Bons Secours Wellness Arena in Greensville, South Carolina, as the Gamecocks' home game. South Carolina won 69-52 last year in Los Angeles and ousted USC 101-61 in the second round of the NCAA tournament. They are 6-0 all-time in the series.

"Now you guys can stop saying who the real SC is, because we are," Gamecocks fifth-year forward Chloe Kitts said to finish off her post-game press conference.

The third matchup within a calendar year was closer than either of the other two with the return of former National Player of the Year JuJu Watkins for the Trojans. She nearly tied the game in the final seconds, bouncing back with a strong fourth quarter that led USC's comeback. But Jordan Lee, a reserve transfer from two-time Final Four participant Texas, recovered from turning the ball over at halfcourt to block the shot, showcasing how the Gamecocks have a roster of riches poised to make a seventh consecutive Final Four.

There is nothing set for future regular-season matchups between the two programs, though Sunday's early season thriller — complete with a special one-off court design — highlighted how spicy it can become with more years behind it.

The Gamecocks may meet the "other" USC there in what would be the Trojans' first Final Four berth since 1986. Here's more from the early matchup of Associated Press top-five teams.

Jordan Lee of South Carolina blocks a shot from Juju Watkins of USC in the second half during their game at Bon Secours Wellness Arena on Nov. 15, 2026, in Greenville, South Carolina. (Photo by Jacob Kupferman/Getty Images)

South Carolina head coach Dawn Staley wasn't concerned about Trojans junior guard Kennedy Smith hitting her groove in the first half with a team-high 15 points on eight shot attempts. That was the game plan. Sophomore Jazzy Davidson and freshman Saniyah Hall are the most talented teammates Watkins has had at USC, and against most teams relying on the 3 will lead to wins.

Three-time champion Staley and an experienced, deep, defensively stout roster absorbed the Trojans' initial punch, but didn't break further while keeping the trio of No. 1-ranked recruits at bay in a 49-45 first half. This is a group that has regularly faced such top talent and walked out victorious. It wasn't shocked.

Watkins eventually found her way to the basket with a strong 11-point fourth quarter that matched her first-half total. She finished with 25 points, but shot 8 of 20 and turned it over five times. Davidson, the 2025 top recruit, had 14 points on a similarly rough shooting line (4 of 14, including 4 of 10 from 3-point range). And Hall finished with 17 points, all but 6 she scored in the second half, and shot 5 of 14. Smith didn't score in the second half and attempted only two field goals.

The Trojans' late offensive push wasn't enough, and even when they thought they were in position to tie or go ahead, Staley pulled out the rug.

Southern Cal coach Lindsay Gottlieb called a timeout after Lee's block with 14 seconds on the clock under the belief the Trojans would have the ball back because it was off Lee. It gave time for Staley, who praised Lee's "spectacular" play, and her coaching staff to quickly review the play and appeal the call.

Video showed the ball going out of bounds off Watkins, which gave South Carolina the ball with a two-point lead. It successfully inbounded, the Trojans were forced to foul Tessa Johnson, and she hit both free throws. Hall missed a 3-pointer in the final seconds.

The "true MVP," Staley said, was video coordinator Hudson Jacob's wife, Rita. She is recovering from surgery, Staley said, and let Jacob drive up to the game.

"He really made the call," Staley said. "It was truly the play of the game. The play of the game. If they would have got the shot up, I'm thinking seeing the 3 go in and then we lose the lead. So shoutout to Rita and Hudson for making a big play for us."

Gottlieb said afterward it wasn't conclusive enough to overrule the call on the floor and questioned how South Carolina could initiate a review, but the Trojans still lost a timeout.

It took a while for Johnson to embrace the "Tournament Tessa" moniker bestowed during the 2024 championship run. She didn't like that she wasn't consistent during the regular season, becoming that version of herself only once the calendar flipped.

The small sample size of the 2026-27 season is evidence that lack of consistent aggressiveness is a thing of the past. The senior guard moved into lead ball-handling duties for the Gamecocks and sparked the first quarter punch that brought them back from an 8-point deficit. She finished with a career-high 28 points with tough finishes at the rim and typical sharp shooting from beyond the arc. She was 9 of 16 overall, 3 of 4 from 3-point range and 7 of 9 from the free-throw line in a game-high 39 minutes.

Johnson averaged career-bests as a junior, moving into the starting lineup and playing all but two games through the national championship loss. Through three games ahead of the USC game, all against ranked opponents, Johnson's averaging a career-high 13.3 points and 4 rebounds with the same 3-point production north of 40% she's had every year of her collegiate career.

Staley is still puzzling together the best combinations of another deep roster, and there is an entire season ahead. Early it's falling on Johnson, junior forward Joyce Edwards and sophomore guard Agot Makeer to lead the way. Edwards had 20 points and 10 rebounds, while Makeer had 9 points on the most efficient performance of the day (4 of 7) with  5 assists.

The Gamecocks rattled off a 10-0 run when Makeer subbed back into the game following  Watkins' free throws at 7:01 of the fourth that cut it to 74-72. Makeer fouled out with 2:10 to play and an 86-77 Gamecocks lead. Watkins cut it back down to two, 87-85, with 46 seconds remaining, and Johnson hit both free throws to ice it in the final 13 seconds.

Even with Makeer and freshman guard Jerzy Robinson (11 points off the bench) fouling out, there are options for Staley. Kitts is back from an ACL tear and scored 15 points with 12 rebounds and 3 assists. She was 4 of 8 and successfully got to the line, where she went 7 of 8. Ashlyn Watkins played 11 minutes, also returning from an ACL. They will both steadily improve as the season wears on.

The Gamecocks were a collective 55.4% and 5 of 10 from 3-point range.

The block by Lee is going to earn the praise for winning the game, but it might not have come down to it if the Trojans offense put it together earlier. They haven't shot well from the perimeter in any of their four games and hit a season-worst 29.6% against the Gamecocks (8 of 27). It was their least efficient game overall by 16%, shooting 29 of 69 overall. Strong first and third quarters ticked up the mark. And they had only eight points from the bench, though the duo of Pania Davis and Laura Williams went 4 of 5 combined.

The free throws are the big ones Southern Cal will want back. They were 19 of 29 from line, which isn't an anomaly in the early part of their season. They're shooting 67.7%  (39th percentile in Division I).

Giannis dove for a loose ball near the floor while two Detroit defenders closed in on him. He kept his balance and flicked the ball behind him toward Thompson in the corner, according to EssentiallySports. The veteran shooter caught it and immediately scored. Klay Thompson called the move an incredible snap that looked like long snapper style. He said it was proof of Giannis' skill level, per the official Miami Heat X account. People often get enamored with Giannis' ability to dunk and run, but his vision is just as deadly.

Before the ball got deflected, Giannis stated he saw Thompson and desired to make the pass. He knew his teammate would stay in the corner because he does not move that much. #2574. Emotional Kirk Cousins: "It's been a tough three years. There's more to the story being written."

Three years ago, quarterback Kirk Cousins played the last game of his first stint with the Vikings at Lambeau Field, tearing an Achilles tendon during a Week 8 game. The first game of his second stint happened on Sunday.

The Vikings won, 30-10, completing the season sweep of the Packers and moving to 7-2 on the season. And Cousins was visibility emotional during his an-field interview after the win with Lindsey Thiry of ESPN.

"It was emotional, you know, coming to the stadium, three years ago, tearing my Achilles here," Cousins said, voice breaking multiple times. "It's been a tough three years,"

Asked whether he thought it would be this emotional, Cousins said, "It's been a tough three years. There's more to the story being written."

It's easier to write the story when the defense is serving up an endless supply of pens, inks, and paper. The Vikings sacked Packers quarterback Jordan Love eight times and forced three turnovers. (The Packers also had a special-teams fumble.)

And while the Minnesota defense did its job (as it always does), Cousins displayed accuracy, velocity, and force on his passes that none of the other quarterbacks on the team could ever match. He also made good decisions in key moments, helping the Vikings' offense convert eight of 15 third-down situations.

It all happened after Cousins showed up only four days before the game. He now has a full week to prepare for a game against the 49ers — the last team he plated during his nine-game run in Las Vegas.

#2573. Ex-Guardians catcher Bo Naylor testifies in defense of Emmanuel Clase, Luis Ortiz in MLB pitch-rigging trial

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Former Cleveland Guardians catcher Bo Naylor on Thursday testified in federal court that he perceived nothing untoward about disputed pitches thrown by former All-Star closer Emmanuel Clase and his former Guardians teammate Luis Ortiz, ESPN reports.

Naylor, who played five seasons for the Guardians, appeared as a witness for the defense in the ongoing federal trial in which prosecutors allege that Clase and Ortiz rigged multiple pitches for the benefit of co-conspiring bettors. In Clase's case, he's alleged to have done so in 17 games across a two-year period beginning in May 2023. Naylor, now a member of the Milwaukee Brewers, was catcher for some of Clase's disputed appearances during that span, including seven of the 18 pitches he's alleged to have rigged.

Naylor, a defense witness, was shown video replays of some of the pitches the government alleges were predetermined by Clase or Ortiz as part of the scheme. Naylor was behind the plate for many of them and said they looked like common sliders outside the strike zone. He said the scouting reports on the hitters Ortiz faced during the two pitches in question indicated that sliders low and away would be a "weapon."

In November 2025, Clase and Ortiz were indicted by the U.S. Attorney's Office for the Eastern District of New York. According to the Department of Justice, both pitchers "agreed in advance with their co-conspirators to throw specific types of pitches and speeds of pitches." The Department of Justice alleged that the pair made at least $450,000 by rigging outings and throwing specific pitches to benefit bettors who wagered on the outcomes of those pitches.

Both Clase and Ortiz pleaded not guilty to those charges in November of last year. Clase and Ortiz have been on administrative leave since late June 2025 while Major League Baseball investigates. MLB has the authority to discipline the pitchers regardless of how the criminal trial plays out.

The pair could face up to 65 years in prison if convicted on the charges of wire fraud conspiracy, honest services wire fraud conspiracy, conspiracy to influence sporting contests by bribery, and money laundering conspiracy.

#2567. MLB rumors: Tarik Skubal's market already hot, contenders eyeing Japanese slugger Teruaki Sato

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

The 2026-27 MLB offseason is a bit more than a week old and already the hot stove moves and rumors are coming in. We've ranked the top 50 free agents and top 25 trade candidates, and built you a calendar of the important offseason dates and deadlines you need to know. Here now are Friday's hot stove happenings.

The market for two-time Cy Young winner Tarik Skubal, far and away the offseason's best free agent, is already hot, according to the New York Post. Skubal is expected to sign in November, before the collective bargaining agreement expires at 11:59 p.m. ET on Dec. 1, though a deal is not imminent. Talks are underway, however, and his market is moving.

Skubal is expected to sign a record contract at least in total value, and possibly in average annual value. Yoshinobu Yamamoto's $325 million deal with the Dodgers is the largest pitching contract ever given out. Max Scherzer and Justin Verlander's matching $43.3 million salaries with the Mets years ago set the record for the average annual value for a pitcher.

The Dodgers, Mets, Padres, Phillies, and Yankees are among the teams linked to Japanese slugger Teruaki Sato, reports the New York Post. Unless MLB and the MLBPA unexpectedly avoid a lockout, Sato must sign before the collective bargaining agreement expires at 11:59 p.m. ET on Dec. 1. Otherwise, he will return to the Hanshin Tigers for 2027.

We ranked Sato as the fourth-best free agent available this offseason, and the best available position player. He has significant power but also swing-and-miss and defensive concerns at third base, similar to Munetaka Murakami a year ago. Murakami slugged 35 home runs in only 127 games as a rookie this season, providing proof of concept for Sato.

The Nationals have signed center fielder Jacob Young to a four-year extension, reports FanSided. The deal is worth $23 million and includes an $8 million club option for a fifth year. The extension buys out Young's three arbitration years and one free agent year, with a club option for a second free agent year. He's now under Washington's control through 2031.

Young, 27, has always been a superlative defender. He unlocked a new level on offense this season, particularly in the second half, when he hit .301 with a .385 on-base percentage. Young had been speculated as a trade candidate since last offseason, but the new extension locks him in as part of Washington's long-term core.

#2566. Kirk Cousins delivers strong first outing as Vikings sack Packers' Jordan Love 8 times

Kirk Cousins delivered in his first start for the Vikings in more than three years.

Cousins, who was traded to Minnesota on Tuesday, delivered a strong performance in a dominant 30-10 Vikings win over the surging Green Bay Packers at Lambeau Field.

Cousins completed 21-of-31 passes for 207 yards and two TDs. He was intercepted once, but the Packers couldn't take advantage of it. Justin Jefferson finished with a game-high nine catches for 77 yards on 13 targets.

Minnesota's defense also made its impact felt, as usual, sacking Jordan Love eight times — the most by one team in the NFL this season. The Packers, who were plus-8 on turnovers this season, were minus-2 in Sunday's loss, with three giveaways. Love rallied in the second half, but it wasn't enough.

The Vikings dominated the first half, taking a 17-0 lead and sacking Love five times. Rookie tight end Mark Redman fumbled on the Packers' second offensive play of the game, leading to a Vikings field goal.

A missed field goal by Packers rookie kicker Trey Smack — his sixth FG miss of the season — also was costly. On the next possession, Cousins hit Myles Price for a 38-yard TD on third-and-23. Price, playing extended snaps in place of Jordan Addison and Jauan Jennings, made the clutch grab, shook his defender and waltzed into the end zone for Cousins' first TD pass since being traded back to Minnesota.

Love drove the Packers into the red zone. But that's when Vikings safety Harrison Smith corralled his 41st career interception, picking off Love in the end zone.

The Packers appeared to pick off Cousins in the second quarter, but he was fortuitously ruled down for a sack. The Vikings then converted a third-and-15 play on the next snap, with Cousins finding Tai Felton on a gorgeous throw, followed by Aaron Jones' 1-yard TD to make it 17-0.

Minnesota kept pressing after halftime. Packers center John Williams helped thwart another promising Green Bay drive by snapping the ball over Love's head, leading to another turnover. The Vikings settled for another field goal and a 20-0 lead.

The Packers tried to fight. Love converted a fourth-and-11 throw to Matthew Golden, and then found J. Michael Sturdivant for the Packers' first score of the game. They forced another Vikings punt and cut the lead to 20-10.

But the Vikings put their feet down. They drove 11 plays and 80 yards, draining nearly seven minutes of clock, and took a 27-10 lead when Cousins found a wide-open Gavin Bartholomew for his first NFL touchdown.

Sturdivant then fumbled the ensuing kickoff, which was recovered by the Vikings, essentially ending any hope for Green Bay. Will Reichard's third field goal of the game pushed the lead back to 20 points and put the Packers down for good.

Matt LaFleur used one of the team's timeouts after the Vikings' third-down carry fell three yards short of the first down line.

Kevin O'Connell opted to go for the win on fourth down and Jordan Mason picked up five yards with 28 seconds left.

Even if Green Bay used its final timeout, Minnesota would have needed to just kneel it once and the game would have been over.

Kirk Cousins is victorious in his return with the Vikings and finished with 207 yards, 2 touchdowns and 1 interception.

Green Bay had the ball on its own 20-yard line facing fourth and 6 trailing by 20. The Packers elected to punt.

Jordan Mason picked up four yards on first down to bring up the two-minute warning. Green Bay has two timeouts left, so a handful of plays/first downs for Minnesota will cement this one.

After the turnover, the Vikings offense took time off the clock. While Minnesota didn't score a TD, Will Reichard kicked a field goal with just under four minutes left to put the Vikings up 30-10.

After the Vikings' TD to move the score to 27 to 10, the Packers were scheduled to get the ball back.

J. Michael Sturdivant, who was the hero scoring a TD for Green Bay earlier, was on the kick return, but fumbled. Minnesota recovered.

Kirk Cousins has thrown another touchdown. This one went to tight end Gavin Bartholomew, who shed a defender and made his way to the end zone for the score.

It was the TE's first career TD, and after the extra point, Minnesota leads 27-10 with 8:29 left in the game.

We head to the final quarter at Lambeau Field and Green Bay is clinging to a 10-point lead.

When play resumes, Minnesota will be facing second and six on their own 33-yard line.

After leading 20-0, the Minnesota lead is down to 10.

Green Bay drove the field and got into field goal range. While the drive stalled, Trey Smack nailed the 40-yard field goal to make it a 10-point game.

After Love's first TD pass of the game, Minnesota looked to respond. Unfortunately, the Vikings couldn't.

Kirk Cousins started the drive with an incomplete pass to Jordan Mason. The RB then picked up eight yards on second down.

Cousins' third-down pass to Justin Jefferson went for just 1 yard, and on fourth and 1 at their own 31, the Vikings elected to punt.

The Packers are finally on board with a touchdown.

Jordan Love found an unlikely target in wide receiver J. Michael Sturdivant, but it worked! Sturdivant scored his first career TD and it was for 32 yards.

It looked like Jordan Love was looking for Tucker Kraft, but the ball bounced through his hands.

The pass then deflected also off of the defender's hands, and somehow bounced right into Savion Williams' hands.

The Vikings weren't able to convert a TD after the turnover, but they still came away with points.

After getting into field goal range, Will Reichard knocked through a 32-yard field goal to increase Minnesota's lead.

The Vikings now lead 20-0 early in the third quarter.

Jordan Love was sacked on the first play of the second half. The Packers offense then moved down the field, until the snap got by Love.

He tried to chase it down, but was unable to wrangle it on the ground, but the Vikings did.

The Vikings lead 17-0 at halftime. The Minnesota defense has been pestering Jordan Love all game.

Love looked shaken up on the Packers' final drive of the first half after he was sacked. The QB was then immediately sacked again, and the Minnesota defense already has five sacks.

Xavier McKinney has six interceptions this season after snagging a pass from Kirk Cousins and making sure to get his feet in.

Green Bay is unable to get anything going consistently against the Minnesota defense.

MarShawn Lloyd had a four-yard run. This was followed by an incompletion, a delay-of-game penalty, and then a 12-yard reception by Matthew Golden that was overturned via replay and ruled an incompletion.

The Packers punted again, and the Vikings led 17-0 with 4:54 left in the half.

It looked like Kirk Cousins had thrown a TD, but the play was reviewed and his knee was ruled down resulting in a sack, but the retaining of possession.

Cousins then hit Tai Felton for a 24-yard completion to get down to the goal line. Aaron Jones then took the carry to the left and took advantage of some great blocking in front of him to score the 1-yard TD.

With 6:17 left in the first half, the Vikings lead 17-0.

After Jordan Love threw an interception in the redzone, the Packers defense held strong and forced a three-and-out.

Green Bay got the ball back. Love had an incompletion and was then sacked on back-to-back plays.

The Packers punted it right back. Love has already been sacked three times this game with 11:39 left in the second quarter.

The second quarter almost could not have begun worse for Green Bay.

The Packers started on the 13-yard line. Tight end Tucker Kraft was whistled for a false start, backing the offense up five yards.

Quarterback Jordan Love then threw an interception in the end zone and it was Harrison Smith who picked off his 41st pass of his illustrious career.

Green Bay is driving as the first quarter ends. When play resumes, the Packers will have it second and nine on the Minnesota 13-yard line, trailing 10-0.

Kirk Cousins' first TD in his return to Minnesota came at an unexpected time. Cousins and the Vikings were facing 3rd and 23 after a facemask penalty.

Under pressure, Cousins got the ball away to the left. Myles Price happened to be turning when he caught it, and the Green Bay defender ended up not tackling him, but pushing him into space. He ran all the way to the end zone for his first career TD.

After the extra point, the Vikings lead 10-0.

#2563. Five under-the-radar MLB free agents who could make a big impact next season

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

The 2026-27 MLB offseason is a little more than a week old now and we're still waiting for the first big trade or free agent signing. That isn't unusual, though. The hot stove, like the regular season, is a marathon, not a sprint. A lockout is expected when the collective bargaining agreement ends at 11:59 p.m. ET on Dec. 1, and there should be a flurry of activity before then.

We ranked the offseason's top 50 free agents, and although it is not a great class, there are dozens of quality players available. You just have to know where to look. Here now are five players who did not rank among our top 50 free agents, but would nonetheless be good options and solid pickups for teams that want to raise their floor and improve their supporting cast.

It was a tale of two seasons for the 29-year-old Bryan Abreu, who had a 5.81 ERA before the All-Star break and a 1.71 ERA after. The under-the-hood estimators, like FIP and xERA, were better in the second half as well, though Abreu lost close to 2 mph off his fastball this year and, not coincidentally, a whole bunch of swings and misses. Abreu is third in appearances and second in innings among relievers since 2022 and it's possible the workload is catching up to him. There's still enough bat-missing ability and late-inning experience here for Abreu to contribute to a contender's bullpen. It just might happen as a seventh-inning guy moving forward, not as the Moment of Truth™ reliever who pitches in the game's biggest moments.

If you're looking for a bottom of the order guy who will take walks and give you 10-15 home runs, that's J.P. Crawford. His defense, specifically his range and arm, has slipped so much in his early 30s that he's no longer a viable shortstop, though he played 33 games at third base this past season. I like him better at second base, but third base works too. Crawford gets on-base at a decent clip and won't strike out excessively, plus he's long been regarded as an excellent teammate and grade-A clubhouse guy. It seems like his time with the Mariners is over and it's for the best. Crawford can go elsewhere, play a new position, and just be part of the lineup rather than one of the faces of the franchise.

Due to injury and ineffectiveness, it looked like Sean Newcomb was on his way out of baseball two years ago. He then reinvented himself as a sinker/curveball guy and carved out a nice second phase to his career as a workhorse utility reliever who won't beat himself with walks (an early career bugaboo) and will limit hard contact in the air. Newcomb, 33, worked at least 90 innings the last two seasons while pitching in every possible role. He closed out games, worked high leverage as a setup guy, soaked up innings in long relief, and opened a few times as well. Newcomb is likely miscast as a go-to bullpen option, though he can be a valuable third or fourth option for a contender. The utility reliever is all the rage these days and Newcomb fits the profile to a T.

Now 35, Emilio Pagán was sensational after returning from a hamstring injury in July, pitching to a 1.88 ERA with 34 strikeouts and only five walks in his final 28 ⅔ innings. The downside is the same as it's always been: Pagán is exceptionally home run prone (career 1.51 HR/9), which is a bad trait for a late-inning reliever who pitches almost exclusively in close games. His fastball remains firm, though, and his splitter is an elite swing-and-miss pitch that allows him to neutralize righties and lefties. As long as you're willing to live with the home run risk, Pagán remains a capable high-leverage reliever, one who is not out of place pitching important innings for a contending team.

Platoon DHs are not the hottest commodity, but Joc Pederson fills the role about as well as anyone in the game. He's a left-handed hitter, so he's on the heavy side of the platoon, and he authored a .245/.338/.496 line with terrific ball-tracking data (exit velocity, etc.) against righties. If you must play him in the field, Pederson can stand in right field or at first base for about six innings before being subbed out for a defensive replacement. He's essentially a bat-only player, though. Pederson will turn 35 in April and he's still a powerful and productive hitter against righties and an elite clubhouse vibes dude.

#2559. Michigan Basketball Bombards William & Mary in Record-setting Performace

Michigan will have to update its record books.

After holding a mere five-point halftime lead, defending college basketball national champion Michigan exploded in the second half for 75 points on its way to a 123-79 win over William & Mary Saturday in Ann Arbor.

It was the most points by Michigan in a single half in school history, and the most points in a game by the Wolverines since 1990. It also tied for fourth place on the all-time single-game scoring output list, matching the 123 points against Illinois-Chicago in 1986.

"The season is going to deliver peaks and valleys, but I think the key is us having a holistic view of we want to be better today than a week ago. And I think we are," Michigan first-year head coach Mike Boynton Jr. said.

"If we continue that growth mindset then I don't know what the ceiling of the team is, but I like the pieces and the ability of this team to find great success as they play more together and get guarded in different ways. "

Michigan (3-1) finished with eight players scoring in double figures – the most in school history. The Wolverines were led by true freshman forward Quinn Costello and transfer center Moustapha Thiam with 16 points each. Thiam also blocked four shots.

Costello canned four 3-pointers and his final one snapped through the net with 5:59 left in the game to give Michigan 100 points and a 30-point lead.

Also finishing in double figures were forward J.P. Estrella with 15, sophomore guard Trey McKenney with 14 and fifth-year guard Roddy Gayle Jr. with 13. Senior point guard Elliott Cadeua, junior forward Oscar Goodman and Kenny Noland scored 11 each. Cadeau also dished out 11 assists and made three steals.

"So much is made about what last year's team did, and that team went through a similar progression, and this team is going through its own evolution.  I'm excited to see where it goes from here," Boynton said.

Michigan played a complete game in the second half and finished shooting 23-of-27 from the free throw line.

William & Mary (2-2) was led by Stas Svika with 13 points and Brian Carter Jr. with 11.

Michigan will travel to face Villanova on Saturday at 7 p.m. on FOX. The two teams met in the 2018 national championship game won by Villanova.

#2557. MLB free agency: Six international players to know for the 2026-27 offseason

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Major League Baseball's free agency period opened earlier this week and teams are now clear to pursue any roster upgrades they deem necessary. That includes players coming over from Japan's Nippon Professional Baseball league, South Korea's Korea Baseball Organization, and Taiwan's Chinese Professional Baseball League. Those are high-level leagues that have sent many impact players MLB's way over the years.

Look no farther than the Dodgers to see how important international talent can be to a club. The Dodgers employed four different former NPB and KBO players this past season, including two-way star Shohei Ohtani, ace Yoshinobu Yamamoto, and starter Roki Sasaki. Ohtani was signed as an MLB free agent, but the others went to the Dodgers through the posting system.

Per the posting agreement with MLB, posted NPB and CPBL players get a 45-day window to negotiate and sign with an MLB team. KBO players get a 30-day window. Players who do not sign during that posting window return to their previous team in NPB, CPBL, or KBO. The MLB team that signs a posted player pays a fee to the player's former NPB, CPBL, or KBO team.

$5M plus 17.5% of contract value over $25M

$9.375M plus 15% of contract value over $50M

For example, the White Sox paid Munetaka Murakami's former team, the Yakult Swallows, a $6.575 million posting fee on his $34 million contract last offseason. That's $5 million on the first $25 million plus 17.5% of the remaining $9 million, which is $1.575 million. The $5 million plus $1.575 million equals the $6.575 million posting fee paid to the Swallows.

Unlike last lockout, MLB will not be pausing the signing window during the expected lockout, according to The Athletic. In other words, if owners lock players out on Dec. 1 as expected, that date will essentially serve as the same deadline for already posted NPB players unless the lockout ends before their 45-day window expires.

There are no superstar-caliber players like Ohtani or Yamamoto available in this winter's international free agent crop. There are, however, several interesting players who can improve an MLB roster in 2027. Here are the six best NPB, CPBL, and KBO players to know this offseason.

Japan's Triple Crown winner hit .306/.383/.609 with 39 home runs in 2026. He has a similar skill set to Murakami but is not exactly Murakami 2.0. He doesn't have quite as much power (but has plenty of it) and won't walk nearly as often, but he does swing and miss a bunch and is unlikely to remain at the hot corner long-term. Sato is a very aggressive hitter who ran a 66% contact rate this past season. That is below the 77% MLB average. The consensus seems to be that he will land at first base or in a corner outfield spot if not next year, then soon. Murakami successfully overcame his contact issues to slug 35 homers in only 127 games in 2026 around a hamstring injury. At minimum, that will have MLB teams reconsidering how they evaluate the Japan-to-MLB transition. Like Murakami, Sato carries risk, and like Murakami, his power makes that risk worth the dice roll. The Hanshin Tigers officially posted Sato on Nov. 1.

Listed at 5-foot-8, Taira gets outlier extension down the mound (close to seven feet despite his height), which creates a low release window. Hitters rarely see the ball come from where Taira releases it. He's not a gimmick pitcher either. Taira sits mid-90s with his four-seam fastball and backs it up with a cutter, sinker, sweeper, slider, changeup, and splitter. The sweeper and slider are distinct pitches, as are the changeup and splitter. The Seibu Lions used Taira as a reliever in 2024 and 2025, then started him in 2026, and he handled the assignment well. The breaking balls are just OK, and the fact of the matter is that pitchers this height don't often hold up under a starter's workload. I would assume the team that signs Taira will give him a chance to start. In the long run, though, he might be a reliever, perhaps even a multi-inning setup man. Taira was officially posted on Nov. 1.

A down 2026 season took some of the shine off Itoh, who won the 2025 Eiji Sawamura Award (Japan's Cy Young equivalent) after throwing 196 ⅔ innings with a 2.52 ERA. To be sure, Itoh pitched well in 2026 (3.18 ERA in 172 ⅔ innings), but he was not as consistently dominant as in the past. The 5-foot-9 right-hander is a seven-pitch pitcher with a low-90s fastball and the usual array of secondary pitches (sinker, cutter, curveball, slider, sweeper, splitter), none of which stands out as a plus offering. Itoh has thrown at least 150 innings in each of the last six seasons. He's seen as a crafty back-end starter in MLB, or perhaps even a reliever (Itoh sat 96 mph out of the bullpen in the World Baseball Classic). The Hokkaido Nippon-Ham Fighters posted Itoh on Nov. 1.

Roh has an unusual agreement with the Hanwha Eagles. He signed the richest deal in KBO history in February (11 years and roughly $23 million), and as part of the deal, the Eagles agreed to post him for MLB teams this offseason, and Roh agreed to return to the Eagles to finish his career when his big-league stint is over. This past season, Roh, 26 in November, authored a .283/.360/.505 batting line with 29 home runs. He has real right-handed power and a good approach at the plate. There are concerns about his propensity to swing and miss as well as his arm at the hot corner. The Eagles formally posted Roh on Nov. 1.

The Seibu Lions posted Takahashi last offseason, but he was unable to find a contract to his liking, so he returned to Japan for another season and threw 148 innings with a 2.64 ERA. Takahashi, 30 in February, is an international free agent now, meaning he does not have to be posted and can instead negotiate at his own pace. More of a ground ball pitcher than a bat-misser, Takahashi sits in the 91-95 mph range with his fastball and has two good secondary pitches in his slider and splitter. He also throws a cutter and curveball. Takahashi is considered a potential innings guy for the back of an MLB rotation.

Tseng pitched for Chinese Taipei in the World Baseball Classic in 2023 and 2026 and he has been one of the CPBL's top relievers the last few years. In 2026, he saved 25 games with a 1.80 ERA and 65 strikeouts in 52 ⅓ innings. Tseng's fastball typically sits in the mid-90s and has run as high as 100 mph in the past, though it has been a few years. His go-to secondary pitch is a breaking ball that needs improvement for Tseng to carve out an MLB career as more than a middle reliever.

#2555. MLB rumors: Why the Dodgers could be Tarik Skubal or bust; Red Sox looking for pitching depth

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

The biggest thing hanging over baseball this offseason is obviously the expiration of the CBA and what everyone assumes will be a lockout. Until then, we'll find out the major award winners this coming week, starting with Rookies of the Year on Monday. And, of course, there's the player movement yet to come.

For the latter, let's round up Sunday's rumors right here.

As we saw plenty in 2026, the Dodgers have a very talented rotation with a few injury-prone parts (Tyler Glasnow, Blake Snell, Shohei Ohtani as a pitcher, etc.). As such, this bit of speculative reporting from The Athletic makes a ton of sense:

The Dodgers will need someone who can cover innings in 2027. It's just a matter of how much they can lean on Justin Wrobleski, trust how Emmet Sheehan finished the season (I'd say probably a good amount), how healthy Gavin Stone is (unknown), how ready Jackson Ferris is (he seems close) and if they have enough depth options behind them.

All that to say, the Dodgers will be in on Skubal. If he goes elsewhere, I don't think it's as simple as the Dodgers going after the next highest-ranked starter on the market, such as a Freddy Peralta or a Michael King. I could see them taking a flier on some depth options to soak up innings in anticipation of a quick ramp-up post-lockout, sort of like they did when they signed Tyler Anderson in the run-up to the 2022 season.

Yes, the Dodgers are in on the Tarik Skubal bidding. We all know that. But if they lose out on retaining the two-time Cy Young winner, they may not just continue moving down the list for available starters. Then again, it's hard to ever know exactly what Andrew Friedman is going to spend money on.

As things stand, the Dodgers' rotation has Yoshinobu Yamamoto, Snell, Glasnow, Roki Sasaki and Sheehan, at least until Ohtani is ready to rejoin the fray.

Coming off two straight Wild Card Series losses and sub-90-win seasons, the Red Sox would surely like to take things up a notch for the 2027 season. One way might be to build out the depth of the pitching staff. They'll be "in the market for a back-end starter" and a right-handed reliever "with swing-and-miss capability," according to MassLive.

For the rotation: Sonny Gray hits free agency, but Garrett Crochet will return from a nearly full-season injury. Payton Tolle and Ranger Suárez fill the 2-3 spots, with Jake Bennett solid as the No. 4. That leaves Brayan Bello, Kutter Crawford and Tanner Houck as options for the fifth spot in addition to depth. It doesn't seem dire, but we've seen plenty of times what kind of havoc injuries can wreak.

In the bullpen, lefty Aroldis Chapman returns at closer with Garrett Whitlock and Erik Miller as setup men. Houck missing out on a rotation spot could mean he helps late as well.

So... who beat out the trimmed-for-space Golden State Warriors and San Antonio Spurs? And who are our losers in a week full of winners? Let's dive into our rankings from the week that was.

No Jalen Williams. No Cason Wallace. No Chet Holmgren. And also, no losses. That's the week that the Thunder just had, first sweeping their season series with the Cleveland Cavaliers before blowing the doors off of the Memphis Grizzlies and Washington Wizards by 70 combined points. Shai Gilgeous-Alexander averaged just under 36 points in the 4-0 stretch, but the story here is Oklahoma City finding a new formula to compensate for all of these absences.

The Thunder built their historic defense around turnover generation, leading the NBA on that front in their 2025 championship season and finishing No. 2 a year ago. They've fallen to 21st as of Sunday, accepting that they simply cannot play as aggressively without their core defenders as they once did. Instead, they're selling out to protect the basket. They allowed the second-fewest points in the paint per game a season ago ... and have trimmed five of them off of their average this season. They've even started Isaiah Hartenstein and Aday Mara together in two of their past three games, though they've shared minimal possessions.

The defense may not be generating turnovers, but the offense isn't committing any either. Oklahoma City has taken its turnover-prevention offense to the extreme. The Thunder are averaging 231.6 passes per game, 10 fewer than any team in the tracking era. Only the Spurs and the Philadelphia 76ers, both healthy championship contenders, are turning the ball over less. This "no passes means no turnovers" offense only works if the individual creators are up to snuff. Gilgeous-Alexander obviously fits the bill, but now, so does Ajay Mitchell. The Thunder are scoring over 1.2 points per possession when Mitchell shoots out of pick-and-roll, good for the 94th percentile league-wide. He's scoring just under 25 points per 36 minutes, more than Cade Cunningham and just below Deni Avdija and Austin Reaves.

Oh yeah, and they made a trade with the Sacramento Kings. I'm comfortable calling any team lucky enough to trade with the Kings an automatic winner for that week, especially when they're acquiring a guard on a rookie contract. Do the words "Tyrese Haliburton" mean nothing to you, Sacramento? Nique Clifford certainly won't live up to that prematurely dealt King, but there's a parallel here to Davion Mitchell, another former first-round pick the Kings dealt who has since blossomed with the Miami Heat. You should trust no team's ability to evaluate players less than Sacramento's ... and no team's more than Oklahoma City's. If Sam Presti thinks Clifford can help the injury-ravaged Thunder, I'm inclined to believe that a price of two second-round picks is a bargain. All in all, it was about as perfect a week as the Thunder could have asked for.

He's averaging 40 points! This isn't a handful of games against terrible teams anymore. The Portland Trail Blazers have been great defensively against everyone except the Los Angeles Lakers because Luka has blitzed them for 94 points in two meetings. Of the 20 highest individual point totals so far this season, Dončić comes in at No. 1, No. 2, No. 5, No. 12, No. 17 and No. 18. The two biggest pillars of the MVP race are scoring and winning. Clearly, he's got the scoring down.

So far, winning hasn't been an issue either. The Lakers are 9-2, and it's almost exclusively because of the offense he runs. As of Sunday, the Lakers ranked 23rd in rebounding rate, 23rd in defense and 25th in turnover rate. It hasn't mattered because the offense is No. 1 with a bullet. The Lakers are roughly 34 points per 100 possessions better when he plays than when he sits, yet they were still able to pull off a critical road win over the Detroit Pistons on Sunday without him. The Lakers are a regular-season wins machine, and Dončić is the engineer.

It's not just the raw total, either. It's how this is all happening. Dončić currently leads the NBA in both 3-point attempts and free-throw attempts. When James Harden was doing that a decade ago, it was considered such witchcraft that defenders started standing behind him and guarding him with their hands behind their backs. I look forward to seeing what sort of nonsense teams concoct against Dončić if this continues. He's making 30-footers look like layups. He's giving Laker fans the sort of individual offense they haven't seen since Kobe Bryant's peak. Enjoy it. Stretches like this don't come around often.

The underlying message of the Ball trade was that the Charlotte Hornets did not think he could be relied upon as a franchise player. Given the questions surrounding his durability, his defense and even his maturity, it wasn't a crazy thought. The idea that he would fare better in a secondary role in Minnesota made plenty of sense. He and Anthony Edwards looked like one of the NBA's best duos in the season's opening week. Then Edwards got hurt, and Ball was suddenly back to being the centerpiece. How has he responded? Well, let's look at the team numbers since Edwards went down:

It's a tiny sample, but thus far, Ball is impacting his new Timberwolves teammates in much the same way he affected his former Hornets (don't worry, we'll get to them!). Everyone else's life gets vastly simpler on offense when they're fortunate enough to play with LaMelo Ball. Even without Edwards, he's more than kept the Timberwolves afloat. When Edwards eventually returns, this team is a genuine contender in the Western Conference.

With Ball, the Hornets had the best offense in the NBA from early December through the end of last season. Well, without him, they're last. By a mile. They're last in basically everything. No team has a lower true shooting percentage. No team turns the ball over. Ready for a jarring stat? We covered Oklahoma City's "no pass" offense earlier. Well, the Thunder are averaging more assists than the Hornets this season ... on 65 fewer passes per game.

The Hornets knew they were getting worse when they made the trade. It was a conscious choice: take a step back, take a few spins in the revamped lottery, accumulate assets that could be flipped later. The Hornets felt like they were destined to be a perpetual middle-of-the-standings team with Ball. They traded him in the hopes that getting worse now could make them championship contenders later.

Their fans probably could have lived with a small step back. What we've seen thus far has been a disaster. Not all of it is their fault. They've barely had Coby White or Kon Knueppel -- and Knueppel will be about another four weeks at least with a hamstring strain. Brandon Miller, the other cornerstone here who just signed a $209 million contract, is shooting 26% from 3 and below 36% from the floor because of how overburdened he currently is. A step back may have been the idea, but nobody thought it would be this bad, nor did many assume Ball would be this good for Minnesota. It doesn't change Charlotte's long-term outlook, but it makes the present that much more painful. All of the goodwill from last year's turnaround has seemingly evaporated.

We came into the season relatively certain about how the Western Conference was tiered. The Spurs and Thunder were at the top. The Lakers, the Wolves, the Houston Rockets and the Denver Nuggets would land between No. 3 and No. 6 in some order. After that? Well, no one gave much thought to the Play-In Tournament. The East was supposed to be the deep conference. That's an opinion we cycle through every four or five years. Every year is supposed to be the East's year, and then it isn't. When the Memphis Grizzlies and Portland Trail Blazers were lighting on the world on fire, it seemed as though the West's depth had triumphed yet again.

It still is, on balance. The Warriors and the Dallas Mavericks, for instance, are strongly exceeding expectations. But the early excitement over Memphis and Portland, at least, is starting to wane. The Grizzlies traded a six-game winning streak for a three-game losing streak. The Blazers walked into the hardest stretch of their schedule thus far, took a loss to the Lakers and then got smacked around by the Spurs. With two games against the Thunder coming, Portland is seemingly coming back down to Earth. For a moment there, the New Orleans Pelicans looked as though they were figuring some things out on a four-game winning streak, but back-to-back losses have them out of the Play-In picture, at least for now.

These teams are still better than we figured they'd be, and there's still a bit of wiggle room in the West. Denver, for instance, looks enormously vulnerable. But the Spurs have won eight in a row. The Thunder have righted the ship. The Lakers, Wolves and Rockets are all as good as we thought or better. For a moment there, it looked like we were due some surprises out West. For now, it seems as though order has mostly been restored.

It is still much, much too early to draw any meaningful conclusions about lottery reform, but an early topic thus far this season has been how bad the bottom of the league still is despite the removal of the tanking incentive. With almost three weeks in the books, there are seven teams with either one or two victories. Between those seven teams, there are only three total victories over teams above .500. The Kings beat the Mavericks ... without Kyrie Irving. The Orlando Magic beat the Toronto Raptors ... without Kawhi Leonard, and their victory over the New York Knicks at least came with Jalen Suggs in the lineup. If Suggs and Paolo Banchero were healthy, the Magic would likely not be in this class.

Essentially, when the worst teams are playing against the best ones at anything resembling full strength, they've been hopeless. Inevitably, a certain number of teams is just going to be bad whether or not they're trying to lose. In fact, given this year's specific outlook, it's not even clear how motivated any of these bottom-tier teams are to actually win. The relegation zone isn't a threat to the Milwaukee Bucks, Brooklyn Nets, Utah Jazz or Los Angeles Clippers because they don't actually control their own first-round picks. You could argue that being in the relegation zone would actually be advantageous to the Chicago Bulls in order to minimize their odds of getting a top-five pick in the bad 2027 draft, because doing so, in concert with their No. 4 pick in 2026, would lock them out of a top-five pick in the stronger 2028 class.

We might not see the sort of overt tanking we've gotten in years past, but the question here is whether or not that will actually matter. With so many of these teams having minimal incentives to win, will they still shut down key players midway through the season? Even if they don't, will attendance and television ratings be better for these teams down the stretch just because they're nominally trying? We're months away from even starting to get answers to these questions, but any notions that reform would create 30 competitive teams have been quickly dismissed. Even in October and November, some teams are already pretty tough to watch.

#2551. MLB rumors: Why the Cubs may already be out on Tarik Skubal, plus latest on Phillies, Cardinals, more

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

The uncertain 2026-27 Major League Baseball offseason is fully underway. The ongoing CBA negotiations and the near certainty of an owner-implemented lockout on Dec. 2 loom over all, and it may indeed mean a flurry of trades and free agent signings leading up to that date. That was certainly the case leading up to the last lockout of 2021-22.

Thanks to that prospect of a hastened pace, offseason rumors are already flowing. Speaking of which, we'll be here each day to round up what's out there. You can find Monday's supply just below.

The expectation remains that we'll see some level of activity on the trade and free agency fronts before the lockout begins in early December. As noted above, that was indeed the case leading up to the last lockout, and this time around, the prospect of drastic changes in the next CBA may have big-spending teams looking to fortify their rosters before those changes are implemented. Speaking of which, MLB Network reports that we could see some notable transactions go down at the upcoming General Managers Meetings, which take place from Nov. 10-12 in Las Vegas.

During a standard offseason, not much beyond behind-the-scenes groundwork goes down during the GM Meetings, and the real moves start happening at the December Winter Meetings. However, unless the lockout is resolved quickly – highly unlikely – then there probably won't be a Winter Meetings this offseason. That means the GM Meetings could be more active than usual.

Free agent ace and, until later this week, reigning back-to-back  American League Cy Young winner Tarik Skubal is the prize of the offseason. The 29-year-old lefty is a fit for any of MLB's 30 teams, but heretofore the most serious bidders have been expected to be the Los Angeles Dodgers (who acquired Skubal from the Detroit Tigers leading up to last season's trade deadline), the New York Mets, and the Chicago Cubs. Now, though, perhaps you can reduce that number of serious bidders to two. While Chicago very much needs rotation help for 2027 and beyond, the Athletic reports that the Cubs "are expected to stay on the sidelines" when the Skubal bidding gets serious. That, no doubt, will come as a disappointment to Cubs fans who are still waiting for the Ricketts to invest in the payroll at levels befitting a big-market contender.

The Cardinals traded away veteran lefty reliever JoJo Romero, along with starter and fellow free agent Dustin May, to the Milwaukee Brewers leading up to the trade deadline. Now, St. Louis may be interested in bringing Romero back on a free agent contract, the St. Louis Post-Dispatch reports.

Romero, 30, is coming off a 2026 season in which he pitched to a 3.36 ERA with a 3.00 K/BB ratio in 55 appearances. In the postseason with Milwaukee, Romero had a 1.13 ERA with 11 strikeouts and one walk in eight innings. He previously spent parts of five seasons with the Cardinals.

Do the Philadelphia Phillies need a new shortstop? That's one of the principal questions of their offseason. Although incumbent Trea Turner is signed through 2033, his defense at the crucial position of shortstop has degraded into "unplayable" territory, and that has the Phils considering fallback options should Turner need to be moved off the position. One option is free agent 31-year-old Ha-Seong Kim, NBC Sports Philadelphia reports. Kim, 32, spent last season on a one-year deal with the division-rival Atlanta Braves. He's been a primary shortstop for five of his six MLB seasons, and while he's certainly not among the very best at the position, he does profile as a major defensive upgrade over Turner. As for the bat, Kim for his career has an OPS+ of 93, and he's capable of stealing a base on occasion. He was, however, an offensive sinkhole for 51 games in 2026. Turner, meantime, may be looking at a switch to the outfield starting next season as the Phillies attempt to keep their contending window open.
